despite my playtime as of the review, ive enjoyed the game. its great! in my opinion, worth the price. sure, it has its vices, what game doesnt? the game isnt realistic to real life hacking, but i think its hard to make a game thats realistic and fun when it comes to hacking and/or programming games as it will be only for a specific audience which reduces who would play and enjoy the game by alot. its a bit repetitive with how hacking to most systems is the same, but i enjoyed many puzzles that this game provided, especially in the labyrinth DLC. this game isnt perfect, no game is but id say its honestly the closest of any games of this genre that i played. the music is one of the few game soundtracks that i actually liked and would listen to in my spare time. the multiple times that arent just port openers are fun and useful!... well most of them (looking at you, Clock.exe). but id say that some are underused, like the log creator and opener, theyre required to be used i think 2-3 times, but the gap between their uses is too big which makes those tools easily forgettable and can make some puzzles hard to impossible without googling how to solve them. id also say that the map can sometimes be hard to use with time, as if youre looking for a specific server, its hard to find it due to there being so many, even with the map organiser tool provided in the labyrinth DLC. i also love how the trace mechanic isnt an immediate game over like in other hacking games where there are also traces, instead you get a saving grace thats (in my opinion) too easy to complete once youve done it once as the process doesnt change if you need to do it many times. i also love how you can use either the GUI or visual part to play the game or the terminal, you are rarely forced to use either. the many customisation options are very fun and well made, they give you a fresh look at your game, either just changing how it looks to where some things are placed. and then theres the story, now im not an emotional personal and ill admit, i havent cried at the ending but i loved it and felt sorry for our favorite guy, especially after the ending cutscene. i had to replay the game to realise that what he meant is that the remaining copy is ours, the actual game. the labyrinth dlc also messes with the games directory, i would have loved to see more of this mechanic but i more than understand why it isnt used as it would likely get annoying. i also really like how there are what i presume are steam keys, i doubt there are any unredeemed keys after 8 years so i dont know what the keys are for, but its a nice gesture. the dev speaking to us after completing the game and letting us know the ips for some fun servers like "cheaters stash" basically letting us get most binary files (port openers and trace stopper) and others. the labyrinths ending is definitely an unexpected twist and while the choice doesnt matter its still nice to have one. i also immensely enjoyed the labyrinth DLC (if you havent noticed already), i enjoyed how the mission and hub actually looked like and the addition of letting us communicate with the others despite our inability to speak. it could also potentially be used if there was a multiplayer, like a race or trying to speedrun many preset missions, either trying to help or stall your friends and you could communicate as a nice feature, maybe making info on server1 vital to help solve a puzzle on server2 or something like that. also the amount of secrets or easter eggs there are is a very nice and fun addition. the shells are imo underused and their trap is rarely used, i think i used it like once or twice on my second playthrough and it actually did something. and there are the fan made DLCs which is great, you can still play even after you complete the actual game.

In short: i enjoyed the game very much, the characters (which are unfortunately few) are lovable. the game has its vices but those are few and often just mild annoyances. ill definitely be replaying the game and its DLC aswell as the fan made ones. its worth its price, but if you think its not for you, you can wait for a discount.

review_text_raw:
The best way to start the review is to mention that this is game is for everyone. It's designed to let even the least "techy" of the players understand the concept and how it works.

As someone who does quite a lot of work on command line on a daily basis, I can definitely say that the game is very friendly in that aspect, and that the developers did a lot of work on making it as realistic as possible, without having the players browse through endless 'man' pages of every command. And it has very positive effects. The simplification of the entire interface, of the commands themselves, makes for a nice introduction for people who never used it before, or for people who have some sort of irrational belief that the command line is only for "hacker gods". People who are already familiar with the command line interface on UNIX based systems will find some of the classic commands returning in this game.

It's not bad at portraying the way most of the black/gray-hat hacking is done. These days, the movies often portray hackers as some wizards who constantly type in various codes on the keyboard while looking at the 8 screen wall with various kinds of text/graphical output, analyzing them in mere seconds and breaking into NASA/CIA/FBI/KGB/<whatever else the movie's plot is about> servers. All that while looking cool. No, no and no. This is not how hacking generally looks like. Instead, as the game itself portrays, hackers merely use (or write) programs with specific purpose (such as PortHack) to do the work for them, while browsing through the Internet, listening to music &c.

Therefore, one could conclude that the game is pleasantly realistic. Yes, some things had to be cut short or ignored. Some tools could hardly work the way they work, or their principle was fixed many decades ago, but it's all excusable, seeing as the main point of the game is providing fun, not having the player spend countless of hours reading stuff on StackExchange and various documentation sites.

Graphics are not the amazing 4k ultra mega sharp masterpiece that in order to run you'd need the latest cutting edge graphics card. They are merely... good enough for the game. It relies heavily on the command line so there is not anything that you could do about it anyway. There are many different themes (packed in the x-server.sys) and each of them has a different background and music.

The music? That's entirely subjective. I did not try a lot of themes, but I could notice that in all of them, the sounds were primarily electronic. Some were pleasant and nice to hear, some were annoying. Personal preference, really. 

The game itself has many references to the real world. These references are based on various movies, games, stores &c. I personally find them as a small nice addition which may or may not give you that "AHA!" moment. Most of them are just hidden in various text files.

With that said, the story of the game is... decent. I do not wish to spoil any of its elements, but let's just say that it's not the most innovative one. It's not a game breaker. It servers well its function to drive the game forward, but don't expect some legendary cool story that will keep you on the edge wondering what will happen next. I did not play the game's add-ons and thus I can't talk about them. Perhaps they are better, or perhaps they are worse.

And now, comes the greatest problem I have found with the game itself. Exactly because the story is the way it is, the game feels too repetitive. It can get boring quite quickly, many times over. While playing the game, you generally have the same routine, hacking into another system (done on the same way almost every time), retrieving/deleting/reading a file, delete the logs, log out. Sure, there are tracers to make the process faster. The firewall analysis can be rather fun when combined with tracers, as you get to feel like some sort of a movie hacker trying to find the right combination while the time is running out. But everything else is, as said earlier, too repetetive and boring.

So when it all comes down to it: 

Gameplay: 6/10
Realism: 8/10
Story: 5/10
Bugs: 9/10 (not a single bug found, although that doesn't mean that one couldn't be there)
Graphics: 5/10 
Music: 6/10
Overall: 6.5/10

I would not recommend you to buy the game with its full price. It's just not worth it. But if you find it to be free, or on sale, and wish to indulge yourself into the world of command line and hacking, then go for it.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. review_text_raw:
Cool Concept, But It Couldn’t Keep Me Hooked

Hacknet starts strong. The idea of diving into a terminal-based hacking sim with a mysterious narrative hook is instantly appealing, especially if you’re into cyberpunk aesthetics or want to feel like a digital detective. At first, typing out real commands and navigating the virtual systems feels immersive and fresh. But that feeling didn’t last long for me.

The main problem is how quickly the novelty wears off. After a couple of missions, the gameplay loop becomes repetitive — scan, probe, crack, read a few emails, rinse and repeat. There’s little variety or meaningful evolution in the mechanics. You’re not solving clever puzzles so much as going through the motions of the same routine over and over.

The story, while intriguing in concept, never really grabbed me. It’s told in fragments through logs and emails, but it lacks emotional weight or urgency. I never felt particularly invested in the characters or their motivations — and a lot of the writing just felt flat.

On top of that, there are some pacing issues. Some tasks feel tedious and drawn out, while others jump ahead abruptly. And if you’re not already familiar with basic command-line structure, the early learning curve can feel more frustrating than fun.

I really wanted to like Hacknet. It nails the aesthetic and tone, and I respect the ambition. But the shallow gameplay and underwhelming story made it feel more like a tech demo than a fully satisfying experience.

I didn't enjoy this game much at all. I like the idea of playing a hacking simulator, but the execution really fell flat. The challenges are monotonous and uninteresting. The files added in for flavor are tired-old jokes. There's not much in the way of story. And the interface is awful. The worst part is the network map where you connect to hosts, which is a crowded bunch of unlabeled dots that you just have to remember, (I eventually gave up and put the list of hosts/IPs into a text document on a second monitor so that I could at least hide the ones I thought I was done with) but the terminal and RAM screens are both pretty bad too. The RAM screen is a combination of an arbitrary hurdle and an excuse to add silly hacker media trope animations, and I want to know what program spends 300MB of ram displaying a short text file. The terminal doesn't scroll or even have history, so once some output goes off the top of the screen it's lost. Did you cat a file and not bother to read it until after rm /log/*; dc;? Have fun breaking back in to get the file again since a bunch of "Deleting file" messages pushed it off the screen? Did you want to !solve because you didn't get everything you wanted the first time you broke in? Too bad.

Definitely not worth the price or your time.

review_text_raw:
I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.

review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

I believe this review to be my first, and let me say this: Hacknet is the most fun I've had with a piece of interactive media in a very long time. It oozes with immersion and masterclass functionality. After Portal 2, most people were left wandering aimlessly along the dunes of the puzzle genre. From time to time, there was an innovative incorporation of puzzle-elements, but never something so powerful. 

GNU/Linux is a UNIX-based mobile, server, office and home desktop operating system. It is built on the powerful and lightning-fast Linux kernel developed by Linus Torvalds in 1996. It's destiny was to maximize productivity and hasten the process of technological evolution. Being lightweight and monolithic, you can take Linux with you wherever you go. When you thought of the internet, you always heard about Linux ever so briefly. 

But recently, things have begun to change. As the corporation gains more control over what we've known to be the internet, people are becoming more concerned. The people want more control over what they rightfully own. Linux offers a full computer suite capable of doing everything a Windows system can do in its own way. This makes Linux a functional choice for people looking for a way out. 

To see such a beautiful piece of technology incorporated into a hacking simulator is beautiful. It's all done so faithfully too. The more I play, the more excited I get. It's fluid, only ever needing so much RAM to operate smoothly. It's also quite responsive, despite some animations taking a lot longer than they should honestly. Another minor flaw is the fact that there's no currency system. There's really only ranking as a reward. It would be cool to make some money and purchase upgrades or better tools.

My final gripe is that some of the missions get a little repetitive. But the story balances things out by keeping it all fresh. There will be funny conversations you can find throughout each system. There's also interesting hide-and-seek style treasure hunts. Listening to cyberpunk playlists really help bring the vibe forward. The interface is extremely realistic.

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1]What is happening in the game:[/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
    [*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
    [*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
    [*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
    [*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
    [*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
    [*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
    [*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
    [*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
    [*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
    [*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
    [*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
    [*]This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.
[/list]

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

Greetings,
BirdCute

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

The whole game is just reading long emails trying to get the important information, then running the same sequence of commands over and over for every challenge. Every time they want to make it harder, they just add one more command to this sequence and repeat the same process.

There was very little problem solving or experimenting happening, which to me is what hacking is all about. Trying things out yourself and learning new tools. Not someone telling you what to do each step of the way.

The terminal interface was neat and the soundtrack was banging, but the game was just too bland and repetitive to be enjoyable.

I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done. As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos, grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly. I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.

The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.

The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.

Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.

Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.

The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.

The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.

In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.

The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

review_text_raw:
After completing Hacknet and it's Labirynths expansion I believe that the game is worth experiencing for the price it asks.

The Good:
- 8h campaign (I did some NOT ALL side missions and the Labirynth expansion)
- Interesting storylines
- Moral Disconnect/Dilemmas
- Simplicity                                   < Easy to understand, just a bit hard to remember commands etc.
- Workshop Support                     < People made some very awesome mods.
- Visuals                                        < It makes your screen look suspicious

The Bad:
- Simplicity
- Slightly difficult to navigate "network map" < Yes I am aware of the existence of the sorter. I still think it could be better in some way.

My wishlist:
- More complexity in the puzzles.
- Clearer more understandable map.
- More ways to solve objectives.
- Hardware Customisation.

Conclusion:
A very pleasant experience with possible extension via the mods on the workshop. Decent story with some interesting twists. The hacking gameplay becomes quite repetitive with time, as it just requires you to think what tool to use for each port. The investigative gameplay is actually surprisingly fun, the game leaves you with enough hints to go on, however the game rarely offers a situation to decide the outcome or change the approach to completing objective. In a certain sense it is linear.

review_text_raw:
Wanted to give this game a shot, and decided to play it for a few minutes to see what it was like.

It's now two hours later and the only reason I'm stopping is that I have to cook dinner.

It takes all the things I loved about Introversion's Uplink, and gets rid of the main issue I had with it. The routing through bundles of servers and having to remove your logs from each and every single server, each and every single time. So tedious it's unbelievable. You still have to remove logs in Hacknet, but thankfully it's a lot more straightforward. This game keeps all the fun parts, the espionage and the feeling of curiosity. There's plenty to read on all the servers, even a lot of flavour text not even related to the game.

Honestly, this is one of the best hacker games I've played, and if my profile is anything to go by, I own most of them available on Steam. It's nowhere near as unforgiving as Hacker Evolution, and nowhere near as tedious as Uplink can get in it's mid to late game.

I can't say too much more without going into spoiler territory, but there's a point about 30-45 minutes in that makes you go "wow... what on earth do I do now?" - and you need to call on all the skills you've learned so far to get past it. The feeling of accomplishment when it works out is amazing.

These guys better be making this into a series like Hacker Evolution, because it has incredible potential, and I'm loving every second.

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1] What is happening in the game: [/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
[*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
[*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
[*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
[*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
[*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
[*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. [*]It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
[*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
[*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
[*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
[*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
[*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

This was Kedeajan,
Have fun!

review_text_raw:
While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer. To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k). Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off. [b]OVERALL[/b]: Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

"Uplink: Hacker Elite" was a fun game because it insulated the gamer from the tedium of command-line driven hacking. Hacknet attempts to do the complete opposite, by adding in copious amounts of esoteric Unix commands.

I only played the game for an hour before applying for a refund. The in-game emails that I read were mundane, as though this game was aimed at juvenile highschoolers ( I'm 40 years old ). One email was about a high school kid making out with a girl and prematurely ejaculating in his pants. Another email was a kid talking about the latest "Call of Soldier" game.

I had to do Google searches, to find out how to hack a firewall and basically gave up trying to figure out how to flood a proxy server.

I dropped out of programming school in real life. Programming & hacking can be quite tedious, which is why Hollywood and Uplink: Hacker Elite try and insulate the user from the realities of hacking.

I'd also like to point out that Uplink featured permadeath... which is where a lot of the tension came from.

review_text_raw:
There is no overarching narrative; you're completing puzzles with no purpose. 

Thus, the puzzles are the focus of the game. However, the puzzles are simple and boring. Simple puzzles can still be interesting. Imagine a child's toy where you fit shapes through their respective holes. You can keep yourself busy for a little bit. This game is similar, but everything is a square. How many times can you fit the square in the square hole before it gets boring? Example: you need the password to decrypt a file and you'll find it on the same system within a file called "password.txt". 

Firewall solving requires no input from the player, it's just a timesink. You call the "analyze" command and wait a few seconds at a time until it reveals the answer. You need to call this command multiple times before it starts to reveal the answer - what gameplay function does this serve? Sometimes you don't have any other task to do while the analyze command is processing, so you just wait and wait.. like an idle game. 

Overloading a proxy server involves clicking a button and waiting a few seconds (depending on the number of shells you have up). There's no depth.

Missions share objectives in the form of notes on your computer. For some reason, the devs thought it was a bright idea to have notes take up a significant portion (~30% sometimes) of your memory. So you often have to write up your own abbreviated notes or you won't have enough memory to run the programs you need to crack the ports. The game is fighting itself.

The UI is a mess. A couple hours and your network map becomes an unintelligible mess with no tools to label systems or otherwise organize it. Missions could at least highlight linked servers.

The music is repetitive. Music can make or break a game. In this case, I found myself shutting off music to play my own playlist in the background so I wouldn't be bored to tears while doing all of the waiting the game requires.

Great idea - terrible execution. For the whole duration of the game you perform same actions again, again and again. And again. Oh, and AGAIN. The totally optional Clicker mini-game and tutorial are the best and most memorable parts of it, and that's saying something.

All of this game's content can be listed as follows:
do {

*check your email, get contract details*
probe
-- Oh, heck, a proxy again.
connect xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect yyy.yyy.yyy.yyy
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect zzz.zzz.zzz.zzz
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect... -- nah, that's probably enough, I still need to "hack" that firewall.
*overloading proxy*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
*Proxy bypassed*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
solve XXXXXXX
WebServerWorm 80
SMTPoverflow 25
FTPbounce 21
SSHcrack 22
*waiting until the end of it*
porthack
*waiting again*
-- Finally.
*doing same repeatative stuff on the hacked machine, clear logs, disconnect*

} while true;

And that's about it. You don't even have to think. At all. More than that, you actually CAN'T think to improve something in your game. Everything you do here is just following instructions like a machine. Bypass Propxy, solve Firewall, open ports, hack ports, get data, clear logs, disconnect, rinse and repeat. Since I didn't actually finish the game, I guess there will be more "hacking tools" introduced, but it won't change anything. The core of the game stays the same - just mindless repetition. This has nothing to do with actual cybersecurity business.

The moral side of some contracts is also questionable, to say the least. They want you to:
- get a private medical card of a person (for the sake of curiosity of some idiot forum-dweller);
- forge a degree for some "ally guy" of the (illegal) group you're working for.
- bring the secret [strike]KFC[/strike]CFC spice recepie out to the public, just, you know, for fun;
And that's only what I've encountered so far.

Some of the more "officially looking" contracts also make little sense. Like the one given to you by a high school administration, where you need to get IT admin password, so the administration can personally investigate a suspicion of IT department sharing student's emails data with outsiders (presumably, student's parents). It's so ridiculously stupid it could actually be another (one of many) dev's attempt at humour.


A word of advice:
If you suddenly became interested in all this "terminal net graph hacker cool" thing, just get VMWare\Oracle, download some Linux distros and build your own virtual network to play with. Way more fun, inherently legal and educative way of spending hours upon hours of your time typing stuff in CLI.

-Addictive
-Characters (you'll see what I mean)

review_text_raw:
[h1][b]IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF A GAME FOCUSING ENTIRELY ON A TERMINAL/COMMAND-LINE AND SOME EASY TO MODERATELY DIFFICULT PUZZLES THROWN IN, YOU MAY LIKE THIS GAME.[/b][/h1]
As someone who has a bit of experience with the UNIX terminal and commands, this game had my absolute full attention and felt familiar to me. [b]I've just recently bought this game (yesterday, at the time of writing) and I was absolutely HOOKED and couldn't get away from it. Hacknet is absolutely my style of game! (right now, I've just beaten the base game and will go through the DLC content shortly. but I may fiddle around with the Extensions)[/b]

[h1][b]TARGET[/b][/h1]
Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. A terminal-based game can seem intimidating or uninteresting to someone who has no experience with it before (and even if you do, a terminal-based game may not be that interesting). If the screenshots and description provided by the game do not capture your attention, it's probably not the game for you. But if your curiosity is piqued, it may be a great experience for you.

[h1][b]PUZZLE ELEMENTS AND TUTORIALS[/b][/h1]
Hacknet introduces itself quite well to the uninformed, and doesn't hand-hold. It throws you straight in after a short tutorial on using the terminal and interface, therefore encouraging experimentation with what you have available. By not holding the player's hand, succeeding in the puzzles without any additional help besides what the game provides will give you a sense of accomplishment. However, that can turn some people off, and if it does, it may not be for you.

It is possible to get stuck in several points in the game, but no solution is too far out there and is solvable without a walkthrough. (and I admit, I have, and have consulted a walkthrough but I was extra careful not to look any further ahead than the current task at hand, most of the time I had just forgotten something simple and was able to get back on track quickly).

The puzzles start off pretty easy, leading you on and increasing the difficulty as it goes, pretty much gently guiding you on how to work with the game's unique nature.

At certain times, the tasks can seem repetitive, and to be fair, it is. You are constantly trying to break into a lot of different computers, servers, devices, etc. but that's what it is. It is an accurate representation instead of the flashy Hollywood style hacking seen on film (but it certainly can be flashy when it wants to be and is for certain parts).

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]
The story itself is nothing outstanding, but it certainly fits the theme and style of the game. It's perfect for the game. The story is there for the beginning and the end of your gameplay, giving you purpose to start and an objective to reach near the end. In the middle of the game, you are given freedom to do what you wish. Or PointClicker, if that's your thing (I won't judge!).

[h1][b]MUSIC[/b][/h1]
The music is an absolute fit for Hacknet and I often found myself focusing on the killer beats rather than what's at hand. It also made me quite shaky during the parts that are time-based.

[h1][b]OVERALL[/b][/h1]
Overall, Hacknet is extremely accurate compared to other things that have tried to display this kind of topic before. The elements work wonderfully and the balance between gameplay and the real elements is on point (all the commands given are used at one point or another and no unnecessary garbage is there). To the average person who may not know anything about the terminal, it can be exciting to get into it for the first time not knowing anything and eventually learn (there may be a little higher risk of getting stuck at a point, but that's okay!). To those who are a little familiar with the terminal and commands, you'll feel right at home and understand the game quickly and have a great time with it!

[h1][b]SHOULD YOU GET IT?[/b][/h1]
If this game looks interesting, [b]IT WILL BE FOR YOU.[/b] The terminal looks intimidating from the start, and if that doesn't deter you and the description of the game brings you in further, you [b]WILL[/b] enjoy it!
