review_text_raw:
*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. review_text_raw:
Premise is engaging and the game is cheap, but it certainly is a no-buy for me.

The game loop goes like this:
[olist]
[*] You receive a contract from one of the many contract hubs in the game.
[*] After receiving it, you will have to hack a computer and gain access to it.
[*] Once you have access, you'll have to search through its folders in order to find information and more nearby computers to hack. You might also find some more new tools.
[*] After you are done, you have to delete the logs of your target computer and disconnect.
[*] If you are not done, hack any remaining computers you found on step 3 until you get the objective done.
[*] Get a new contract.
[/olist]

Hacking progress goes like this: remote computers have a different number of closed ports which you have to open with commands that you acquire as you progress. Each open port lowers the toughness of the target computer and, once it's low enough, you can use a magic command to hack it and gain access to its contents. There are a few extra things (proxies, firewalls, time limit and some per-mission modifications) but overall the process is tedious and revolves around repeating the same commands over and over.

Some other reviews mention that this game has some learning potential, which is wrong. The commands that you execute take no arguments and just show progress bars which go up at the same constant rate, forcing you to be glaring at your screen until they are done. Any resemblance to an actual UNIX command is just the fact that they are, indeed, executed on a terminal emulator.

The game got tedious after an hour. If you enjoy the loop, you might enjoy the game, but be advised that it is repetitive, almost non-interactive and a bit dull. The story is not engaging at all and just revolves around people asking you to hack things.

review_text_raw:
[b]A HACKER GROUP SEARCHING THE TRUTH[/b]
[i]Hacknet[/i] was available for free in Humble Bundle for a short period, long time ago. It's one of those game that normally I wouldn't buy. The game is centered on group of hackers that receives some contracts from people that wants to obtain something: it could be retrieving a file or cancel something from another user computer. For the entire game, you will see the Hacknet OS, a system that allows to execute some tools and let you inside other networks and devices.

[h1]VERY REPETITIVE GAMEPLAY[/h1]
At the beginning [i]Hacknet[/i] seems promising. The game make you feel like you are a real hacker, trying to break in other people computers, but after a while everything repeat itself. You always do the same things: hack devices ports, with specific executables that you just need to download from the hacker group server, once you are in, you need to check the files, and once you completed the task, simply reply to the client request mail, with details needed. Some of these contract are challenging and it will take a lot of time, trying to understand which is the solution of the enigma. Usually there is not only one way to go, but you can complete the mission in different ways. The real problem is that missions are all the same and nothing really change for the whole game.

[h1]CANCEL THE LOGS[/h1]
One of the things that the game never stop to stress you out is deleting the logs in a computer after you finished to snoop around. At the beginning I did it, because I was scared that I could be traced, losing the mission. After a while, because you have so many steps to do in order to complete the contract, I forgot to clean them several times, and nothing happened. They cannot trace me so I simply stopped to worry about it: I canceled only when I remembered.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
[i]Hacknet[/i] could have potential. It looks different and interesting, but, as I've mentioned before, you need to do always the same bunch of actions, and this made me lose the interest in the game. I have still to complete the main story, but I think I played enough to express an opinion on this title. I really wanted to buy also DLCs, but after this experience, I think I stop here my experience with this game.

[h1]10/10 will play again & buy the DLC when I have money[/h1]

I got a free copy of [i]Hacknet[/i] from a promotion on Humble Bundle without really knowing what the game was and only started playing it because of the Spring Cleaning Event here on Steam. I only intended to play it for a little bit and then move on to something else.  ...I finished the game in one sitting. Which took most of the night when I was supposed to be sleeping and I barely even noticed. Never before would I have said that a game based almost entirely around typing computer run commands would hold my interest, but [i]man[/i] was I completely enthralled start to finish.

Not only did I finish the game in one sitting, but I also immediately started over to complete side quests and find bonus material I had missed the first time around. I still haven't finished the last achievement and found all the cool hidden bonus stuff.

[u]Plot[/u]
You have been introduced into the world of hacking by Bit, another hacker who has sent you a series of automated messages fearing his own demise. [spoiler]Yes, he is actually dead. I was about an inch away from crying when it was finally confirmed late in the game.[/spoiler] Through the course of the game you work with a number of hacker communities working both as a freelance digital vigilante and trying to unravel what really happened to Bit. The plot was exciting and I ended up emotionally invested. [spoiler]There is only one ending to the game, but there are optional side quests that alter way in which you get there, as well as bonus content that appears to only be available after a restart.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Most of the gameplay is done by typing various commands into your "terminal" in much the same fashion as old-school computer programs. If you've worked with DOS or similar systems you will probably have a bit of a leg up with the basic mechanics of the game. Using those commands you hack through the security systems of other computers, copying and deleting files off their harddrives and skipping from their computers to others in their network. These hacking attempts are sometimes straightforward, sometimes more complicated with critical thinking and puzzle cracking abilities required. The further you progress in the game the more difficult they become with most of the later hacking attempts becoming a fast-paced, speeding heart race against time. There is one(?) hidden mini-game that differs from this format. [spoiler]You can find it by taking the "Pointclicker" contract from Entropy[/spoiler] Overall, I didn't think the game was very difficult, although there were plenty of challenges to overcome. I did require a walkthrough the get myself out of a tricky spot, but that was mostly due to impatience. Probably the most difficult thing in the whole game was typing commands fast enough, so those who aren't good typists might struggle more with this game.

[u]Graphics & Music[/u]
[i]Hacknet[/i] has a very simple GUI for the entire game, fairly old-school computer but with a futuristic vibe. If the color scheme bothers you, just pay attention to the achievements. ;) [spoiler]My favorite was the L-e version, I do believe.[/spoiler] The music was all low-key techno music which I quite enjoyed. Sometimes it got a bit repetitive, but it changed according to where you were in the questline, so as long as you didn't get stuck in one place for a long time (like I did, before giving up and finding a walkthrough) it was fine.

[u]Bugs & Performance[/u]
Performance wise, the game ran perfectly well on my potato laptop with only 3GB of RAM. Since the game is done almost exclusively with the keyboard, having a real one is a must IMHO, but a mouse isn't necessary. I did just fine with a trackpad. The only "bug" I encountered when playing the game is that the game crashed whenever you tabbed out of it in fullscreen mode, even if you were chilling on the main menu. So make sure you save the game before attempting to open a different window!

review_text_raw:
Overview:
  Hacknet is at its heart a digital exploration game. Using a powerful suite of programs that you gain throughout the game, the player must gain access to systems and perform contracts. The game has a very similar feeling to the older game Uplink and hacking is done through speed, knowledge of your tools, and system resource management (RAM).

Plot:
  The plot is pretty threadbare, but does a good job of pulling the overarching story together. The ending makes sense, but is a little lacklustre for the scope of what you supposedly accomplish. However, this is in character for hacking since public attention is bad for those at the fringe of legality. Overall, I enjoyed the plot, but the beginning intro and ending are really the only interesting points. It's difficult to do characterization when all you have is text, but I felt that more effort could have been put into letting the player get to know more of the other people in the story (naix, maybe some backstory on bit, etc.)
 
Gameplay:
  The gameplay is separated into two parts: hacking and forensics. The actual hacking is rather easy since most trace timers last far more than long enough and some systems actually keep your admin after you disconnect. The main challenge in this format is simply knowing which order to run the port hacking programs in so that you can maximize efficiency and minimize time spent not logged in. These do get quite intense at times and a few conflict sequences definitely run the point home that you're not invulnerable. Progress through the game is blocked in a sort of metroid-vania way, in the sense that you need this power to unlock that type of port to enter. I enjoyed this, but wished that there were more early systems that you needed to backtrack to.

  That backtracking is part of the second part of the gameplay, the forensics. By this I mean that you spend your time going through file systems trying to spot the file with the password, scanning computers to reach connected nodes, and searching for new IPs to check out. In fact, there is an entirely alternative gameplay path that is only reached with diligent use of your tools. I loved the exploring, but it did feel quite limited, or at the very least truncated to be more accessable for players who might not be used to the gameplay style.
  Part of the joy of the exploration comes from the humor that you find in random files. From a script for "Titanic 2" that involves the icebergs running onto land and attacking people to Bash.org IRC logs, there is a decent amount of silliness and joy to discover. Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

review_text_raw:
This might just be the 10 years since launch, or my actual experience with computers, but the gameplay loop feels a bit off (pun not intended) for me. The tutorial got me curious enough with the plot to get through, but there is no substance in the base game. Haven't played the DLC, not interested.

If you are into looking at hacker-looking interfaces and typing the same half a dozen commands over and over (tab complete and up key for history available), you will enjoy it. If you want anything that is anymore puzzling than following clear instructions, look elsewhere.

Basically: 1- open an email, 2- click email attachments for a target IP and maybe add a mission summary note to the screen, 3- click a button to connect to said IP and click another button to Probe the system, 4- run the same 2-5 commands on the same list of ports, 5- browse the filesystem to either find or place a file at mostly the same folders, 6- erase all logs and disconnect, 7- repeat. That's it. The game has a simplified terminal emulator missing a few basic features but fine, you can mostly use it to get things done instead of the GUI except when emailing (mostly). There are no puzzles, the exploits are literal executables you run and wait, the only variability is whether the target machine has proxies or a firewall then you gotta login into a bunch of places you already hacked first and run a shell overload (run and wait) then run a firewall analyzer to unscramble a keyword (run and read). Sometimes you gotta disconnect before a tracing timer runs out, which is never an issue until a single mission has like a 3 seconds timer but same difference. If you do *somehow* get traced, you might need to do the one different thing and change your IP address by... following steps 1 through 6! Or just reboot. Yeah, that's it: steps 1-7, sprinkle disconnects according to timer and if something fails just reboot and resume as usual is the whole game. There are two routes if you accept an optional mission but rest assured, same gameplay eveywhere.

This is a pretty good puzzle-ish game all things considered, but I put this as recommended only on the condition that this game is on sale for $5 or less. The game introduces new quirks and puzzle elements at a steady pace, and there are certain points where you need to apply everything you learned and think outside the box to progress - the feeling you get after figuring it out is really satisfying. The problem is that even though you're given new things to play with, in the end it's all the same. You're given four different exe files gradually that can render a security system vulnerable, but you simply type their filenames and execute them. That's what most of the game is, typing the same things over and over again. Some text files you find in the victims' computers are amusing and some emails are funny, but that's as diverse as it gets.

Pick it up if you want some fun for two hours or so, but this is definitely not a game I'd value at $10. The only reason I got it was because Steam had a weekend where you can keep the game permanently if you simply downloaded it.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is pretty much what it says on the tin - a hacking-themed game in which you must meet escalating challenges throughout the course of its story, which opens with a posthumous message coming from a hacker who has disappeared.  Stop right there, though - the story isn't very strong on the conspiracy and ends up being a missed opportunity, so don't dive in just yet.

Those not familiar with command-lines need not fret as this isn't a full-blown OS simulator like other games in the genre.  While it does have its own level of CLI sophistication, the tutorial and pacing thereafter is carefully crafted as not to overwhelm the inexperienced.  Anyone looking to roleplay a super hacking machine can comfortably play this game without having a manual in front of them (though a notepad may help).  Rather than have you coding a bunch of exploits or what have you, your hacking terminal - which is beautifully-rendered, btw - is loaded with magical tools that do all the work for you.  You just need to handle the set up, if you will, and the software will do the rest.

What separates Hacknet from others in the genre is its combo of command-line terminal and graphical user interface (think X-Window).  The game is aesthetically pleasing to the eye with a mix of hi- and low-tech, giving the interface an authentic OS feel.  If you're not keen on typing every little thing (which you can absolutely elect to do), you can instead click on the GUI to navigate around most of the systems and poke around.  You'll still need to key in some commands, but there's a good balance here if you want to save some time with navigation and reading files.  Websites aren't functional, but they do appear in the game and give it that extra little flavor, with one exception being a Clicker game that you can waste time on should you so choose to.

So while the story doesn't really play out in the best of ways, the hacking is quite fun... at least for the first little bit.  It very soon becomes repetitive because ultimately the puzzles are limited.  You will be taking on contracts/jobs from message servers and they each boil down to a) get into the target system and b) grab some information or delete stuff. I'm currently 3-4 hours into my play through and I would say I have encountered 1 scenario which was different from all the rest which honestly might have been me messing up. I basically lost my desktop environment, so I had to rebuild from the terminal. Speaking of the terminal this game is basically terminal simulator, although as long as you have your desktop environment you can also simply click a lot of things.

I haven't really experienced any increase in difficulty in my time playing this game, despite the fact that you're supposedly moving onto more and more elite hacker group with harder hacks/challenges. The only thing that gets 'harder' is the qualification challenges to enter into said groups, but once you're in them the quests they provide are all quite simple.

This game basically is an exercise in tedium. You do the same thing over and over again with very little to no engagement on your end. Your tools carry you, they take care of all the heavy lifting. As long as you can 1) gather sufficient tools for the job and 2) know how to employ those tools (what to type in the terminal), you are set. Your tools do all the work completely by themselves once you've deployed them. I haven't seen them fail once, nor has there ever been a requirement for manual intervention to prevent them from failing.

There's another review on this page from a reviewer who claims to have completed this game and has a total of 10 hours of play time, so there's not a lot of content either. In conclusion this game at best will teach you very basic Linux commands (a lot of them aren't even available in the game) that can be entirely avoided by simply just clicking stuff.

review_text_raw:
"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.
